claim: MAPT is highly expressed in the brain, and there is little expression in other tissues.
source: MAPT is highly expressed in the brain, and there is little expression in other tissues.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, which displays TPM values across tissues, and is explicitly stated in the figure caption.

claim: The median PSI of exon 10 among all tissue samples is 0.54.
source: The median PSI of 0.54 among all tissue samples is indicated by the red dotted line.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the figure caption and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 75% of samples were within an SD of the median PSI of 0.54.
source: However, 75% of samples were within an SD of the median PSI of 0.54, demonstrating that the 3R to 4R isoform ratio was close to 1:1 among individuals and across tissues.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of GTEx data presented in the Results section.

claim: The normal ratio of 3R to 4R isoforms is approximately 1:1.
source: The normal ratio of 3R to 4R isoforms is approximately 1:1 (Hefti et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hefti et al., 2018.

claim: Twenty-nine clinically validated disease-causing mutations have been identified in the region of the exon 10 – intron 10 junction.
source: Twenty-nine clinically validated disease-causing mutations have been identified in the region of the exon 10 – intron 10 junction (Stenson et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stenson et al., 2003.

claim: 20 of the disease-associated mutations deregulate MAPT pre-mRNA splicing altering the ratio of 3R to 4R.
source: Although some mutations alter the Tau protein sequence (Mirra et al., 1999; Iseki et al., 2001), 20 of the disease-associated mutations deregulate MAPT pre-mRNA splicing altering the ratio of 3R to 4R (Hutton et al., 1998; D'Souza et al., 1999; Hasegawa et al., 1999; Jiang et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The median in-cell DMS reactivity of the mature MAPT isoforms was 0.22.
source: The median in-cell DMS reactivity of the mature MAPT isoforms was 0.22, significantly greater than the median in-cell DMS reactivity of the SSU, which was 0.008 (Figure 1—figure supplement 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental DMS-MaP data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7C.

claim: The median in-cell DMS reactivity of the SSU was 0.008.
source: The median in-cell DMS reactivity of the mature MAPT isoforms was 0.22, significantly greater than the median in-cell DMS reactivity of the SSU, which was 0.008 (Figure 1—figure supplement 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental DMS-MaP data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7C.

claim: Approximately 89% of base pairs were contained within the exon units in the 4R isoform.
source: In the 4R isoform, approximately 89% of base pairs were contained within the exon units; only 11% of base pairs were between residues from exon 10 with those of exon 11 (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: Only 11% of base pairs were between residues from exon 10 with those of exon 11 in the 4R isoform.
source: In the 4R isoform, approximately 89% of base pairs were contained within the exon units; only 11% of base pairs were between residues from exon 10 with those of exon 11 (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: The mature exons fold as independent structural units.
source: This result suggests that the mature exons fold as independent structural units.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that most base pairs are intra-exon.

claim: DMS reactivity in exon 10 was significantly lower for the pre-mRNA (median in-cell DMS reactivity: 0.08) than for the 4R isoform (median in-cell DMS reactivity: 0.22).
source: However, when we compared DMS reactivities for pre-mRNA and the mature 4R isoform, we found that DMS reactivity in exon 10 was significantly lower for the pre-mRNA (median in-cell DMS reactivity: 0.08) than for the 4R isoform (median in-cell DMS reactivity: 0.22) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental DMS-MaP data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The pre-mRNA is more structured than mature mRNA independent of protein protection.
source: The pre-mRNA is thus apparently more structured than mature mRNA independent of protein protection.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of in-cell and cell-free DMS reactivity data.

claim: In the +19C>G mutant that strongly favors the 3R isoform, more than 55% of structures belong to cluster 1, which is defined by a fully base-paired 5' splice site.
source: By contrast, in the +19C>G mutant that strongly favors the 3R isoform (Tan et al., 2019), more than 55% of structures belong to cluster 1, which is defined by a fully base-paired 5' splice site (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural ensemble analysis shown in Figure 2D and cited experimental data from Tan et al., 2019.

claim: Greater than 50% of structures in the ensemble of the +15A>C mutant (cluster 5), which shifts the isoform balance entirely to 4R, were characterized by lower ΔG‡ of unfolding for the splice site region.
source: Conversely, greater than 50% of structures in the ensemble of the +15A>C mutant (cluster 5), which shifts the isoform balance entirely to 4R (Tan et al., 2019), were characterized by lower ΔG‡ of unfolding for the splice site region (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural ensemble analysis shown in Figure 2B and C and cited experimental data from Tan et al., 2019.

claim: Mutations shift the structural ensemble of the MAPT exon 10 – intron 10 junction, and these structural shifts correspondingly change exon 10 splicing.
source: Based on these results, we concluded that mutations shift the structural ensemble of the MAPT exon 10 – intron 10 junction, and these structural shifts correspondingly change exon 10 splicing.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the structural ensemble analysis and experimental splicing data.

claim: The number of pre-mRNA nucleotides, as observed in each structure, increased through the splicing cycle.
source: The number of pre-mRNA nucleotides, as observed in each structure, increased through the splicing cycle (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Unfolding larger regions around the 5' splice site improved the predictive power of the model, and the Bact complex footprint yielded the best prediction accuracy (R2=0.89).
source: Unfolding larger regions around the 5' splice site improved the predictive power of the model, and the Bact complex footprint yielded the best prediction accuracy (R2=0.89; Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Using features of the distribution of unfolding ΔG‡ in the structural ensemble produced greater predictive power than simply using the unfolding ΔG‡ of a single minimum free energy structure.
source: Crucially, we found that using features of the distribution of unfolding ΔG‡ in the structural ensemble produced greater predictive power than simply using the unfolding ΔG‡ of a single minimum free energy structure, supporting the importance of RNA ensemble behavior to splicing outcome (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of modeling approaches shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Synonymous mutations that alter exon 10 inclusion lie a mean distance of 54 nucleotides from the exon-intron junction.
source: Synonymous mutations that alter exon 10 inclusion lie a mean distance of 54 nucleotides from the exon-intron junction, whereas those in the intron are a mean of 14 nucleotides from the junction.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of mutation positions.

claim: Intronic mutations that alter exon 10 inclusion lie a mean distance of 14 nucleotides from the exon-intron junction.
source: Synonymous mutations that alter exon 10 inclusion lie a mean distance of 54 nucleotides from the exon-intron junction, whereas those in the intron are a mean of 14 nucleotides from the junction.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of mutation positions.

claim: The model performed well for compensatory mutations (median bootstrapped R2=0.76).
source: Although the model performed well for compensatory mutations (median bootstrapped R2=0.76), it yielded significantly less accurate predictions for non-synonymous mutations (median bootstrapped R2=−0.21) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: The model yielded significantly less accurate predictions for non-synonymous mutations (median bootstrapped R2=−0.21).
source: Although the model performed well for compensatory mutations (median bootstrapped R2=0.76), it yielded significantly less accurate predictions for non-synonymous mutations (median bootstrapped R2=−0.21) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: Using splice site strength as the sole predictor yielded poor prediction of exon 10 PSI for all mutation categories.
source: We found that using splice site strength as the sole predictor yielded poor prediction of exon 10 PSI for all mutation categories (Figure 4B; Equation 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was a weak positive correlation between PSI and enhancer strength.
source: There was a weak positive correlation between PSI and enhancer strength and a significant negative correlation between PSI and silencer strength (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There was a significant negative correlation between PSI and silencer strength.
source: There was a weak positive correlation between PSI and enhancer strength and a significant negative correlation between PSI and silencer strength (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: When exon 10 PSI was modeled with the changes to the motif strength of all SREs, prediction accuracy increased (R2=0.51) compared with that obtained when only splice site strength was considered (R2=0.29).
source: When exon 10 PSI was modeled with the changes to the motif strength of all SREs, prediction accuracy increased (R2=0.51; Figure 4C) compared with that obtained when only splice site strength was considered (R2=0.29); for non-synonymous mutations accuracy was even higher (R2=0.75).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: For non-synonymous mutations, prediction accuracy using SRE motif strength was R2=0.75.
source: When exon 10 PSI was modeled with the changes to the motif strength of all SREs, prediction accuracy increased (R2=0.51; Figure 4C) compared with that obtained when only splice site strength was considered (R2=0.29); for non-synonymous mutations accuracy was even higher (R2=0.75).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A combined interactive model consistently produced more accurate predictions of exon 10 PSI compared with a structure-only model and an SRE-only model for all mutation categories (R2=0.89).
source: Indeed, a combined interactive model consistently produced more accurate predictions of exon 10 PSI compared with a structure-only model and an SRE-only model for all mutation categories (R2=0.89; Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: An alternative additive model had lower prediction accuracy (R2=0.80).
source: An alternative additive model had lower prediction accuracy (R2=0.80) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), particularly for non-synonymous mutations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: For about 51% of mutations, both structure and SRE motif strength were altered in the same direction to either promote or inhibit exon 10 inclusion.
source: For about 51% of mutations, both structure and SRE motif strength were altered in the same direction to either promote or inhibit exon 10 inclusion (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: For 17% of mutants, structure dominated the direction of splicing.
source: For 17% of mutants, structure dominated the direction of splicing.
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: For about 23% of mutants, SRE strength was dominant.
source: For about 23%, SRE strength was dominant (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Most mutations should result in inclusion of exon 10 according to the model.
source: Our model predicted that most mutations should result in inclusion of exon 10.
evidence: The claim is supported by in silico mutagenesis analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: About 75% of known disease-associated mutations in this region induce exon 10 inclusion.
source: This bias is consistent with the observation that about 75% of known disease-associated mutations in this region induce exon 10 inclusion (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of disease mutations shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A significantly greater proportion of disease-inducing mutations (76.4%) results in changes to both structure and SRE compared with uncategorized mutations (36.0%).
source: We found that a significantly greater proportion of disease-inducing mutations (76.4%) results in changes to both structure and SRE compared with uncategorized mutations (36.0%) (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mutations that alter both structure and SREs have a greater likelihood of causing disease than mutations that alter only structure or only an SRE.
source: Thus, mutations that alter both structure and SREs have a greater likelihood of causing disease than mutations that alter only structure or only an SRE.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the statistical analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mutations overall caused a slight skew toward a more structured exon-intron junction that would be expected to decrease inclusion of exon 10.
source: Intriguingly, mutations overall caused a slight skew toward a more structured exon-intron junction that would be expected to decrease inclusion of exon 10 (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B); however, these same mutations altered SRE strength in a manner that skewed toward increased inclusion of exon 10 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), indicating that SREs act to counter the effect of structural changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by in silico mutagenesis analysis shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mutations altered SRE strength in a manner that skewed toward increased inclusion of exon 10, indicating that SREs act to counter the effect of structural changes.
source: Intriguingly, mutations overall caused a slight skew toward a more structured exon-intron junction that would be expected to decrease inclusion of exon 10 (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B); however, these same mutations altered SRE strength in a manner that skewed toward increased inclusion of exon 10 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), indicating that SREs act to counter the effect of structural changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by in silico mutagenesis analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and is an inference about the role of SREs.

claim: The mean exon 10 PSI for VUSs was 0.66.
source: The mean exon 10 PSI for VUSs was 0.66, and 70% were within an SD of the mean (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of VUSs shown in Figure 6D.

claim: 70% of VUSs were within an SD of the mean PSI.
source: The mean exon 10 PSI for VUSs was 0.66, and 70% were within an SD of the mean (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of VUSs shown in Figure 6D.

claim: All six VUS predictions were correct.
source: We found that all six predictions were correct (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental validation shown in Figure 6E.

claim: In-cell chemical probing of the endogenous MAPT pre-mRNA provided strong evidence for formation of this hairpin in cells and for structural features not previously captured.
source: Our results suggest that this is not the case for the exon 10 – intron 10 junction region: in-cell chemical probing of the endogenous MAPT pre-mRNA provided strong evidence for formation of this hairpin in cells and for structural features not previously captured.
evidence: The claim is supported by DMS-MaP data presented in the Results section.

claim: In cells, exonic regions were less structured than introns.
source: Our analysis also revealed that, in cells, exonic regions were less structured than introns, as also observed by Sun et al., 2019.
evidence: The claim is supported by DMS-MaP data and cited work from Sun et al., 2019.

claim: Mature MAPT 3R and 4R are less structured in the region of exon 9 through exon 11 than is the pre-mRNA.
source: Mature MAPT 3R and 4R are less structured in the region of exon 9 through exon 11 than is the pre-mRNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of DMS-MaP data for mature and pre-mRNA.

claim: Most base pairs are intra-exon in mRNAs which encode yeast ribosomal proteins.
source: Specifically, mRNAs which encode yeast ribosomal proteins that indicate that RNA folding in both pre- and post-spliced exons is highly local and that most base pairs are intra-exon (Zubradt et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zubradt et al., 2017.

claim: If the 5' splice site was always paired, only the 3R isoform would be produced.
source: If the 5' splice site was always paired, only the 3R isoform would be produced.
evidence: The claim is a logical inference based on the mechanism of splicing.

claim: The presence of 3R and 4R isoforms, usually in a 1:1 ratio, implies that the junction is accessible in a subset of the structures.
source: However, the presence of 3R and 4R isoforms, usually in a 1:1 ratio, implies that the junction is accessible in a subset of the structures.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed isoform ratio and structural ensemble analysis.

claim: Disease-causing mutations produced distinct shifts in the ensemble of the MAPT exon 10 – intron 10 junction region.
source: We found disease-causing mutations produced distinct shifts in the ensemble of the MAPT exon 10 – intron 10 junction region; these shifts showed strong correlation with changes in the 3R to 4R isoform ratio and confirmed that ensembles are essential at this junction.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural ensemble analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: These shifts showed strong correlation with changes in the 3R to 4R isoform ratio and confirmed that ensembles are essential at this junction.
source: We found disease-causing mutations produced distinct shifts in the ensemble of the MAPT exon 10 – intron 10 junction region; these shifts showed strong correlation with changes in the 3R to 4R isoform ratio and confirmed that ensembles are essential at this junction.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural ensemble analysis and experimental splicing data.

claim: The U1 snRNA base pairs with a nine nucleotide sequence around the exon-intron junction.
source: The U1 snRNA base pairs with a nine nucleotide sequence around the exon-intron junction (Roca et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Roca et al., 2012.

claim: A large region of the pre-mRNA interacts with the spliceosome and must be unfolded during splicing.
source: However, our analysis of cryo-EM structures of the human spliceosomal assembly cycle revealed that a larger region of the pre-mRNA interacts with the spliceosome and must be unfolded during splicing.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The structural model performed most accurately when 43 nucleotides around the 5' exon-intron junction were required to be unfolded, corresponding to the region within the spliceosome Bact complex.
source: Our structural model performed most accurately when we required 43 nucleotides around the 5' exon-intron junction to be unfolded, corresponding to the region within the spliceosome Bact complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: This observation suggests that a large region of the pre-mRNA is dynamically remodeled by the spliceosome and that structures distal to the exon-intron junction can regulate splicing.
source: This observation suggests that a large region of the pre-mRNA is dynamically remodeled by the spliceosome and that structures distal to the exon-intron junction can regulate splicing.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the modeling results.

claim: mRNA unfolding and accommodation into the Bact complex are a key rate-limiting step in splicing.
source: Rather, our model argues that mRNA unfolding and accommodation into the Bact complex are a key rate-limiting step in splicing, and considering this step is necessary to accurately model splicing outcome for a diverse set of mutations.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the modeling results.

claim: For both translation initiation and splice site selection, there is a region in which RNA structure functions as a rheostat.
source: Broadly, our definition of a functional footprint for splicing parallels a similar idea for translation initiation by the ribosome (Corley et al., 2017; Mustoe et al., 2018a; Mustoe et al., 2018b), for which the footprint is roughly 30 nucleotides. Thus, for both translation initiation and splice site selection, there is a region in which RNA structure functions as a rheostat.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on comparison with translation initiation and supported by citations.

claim: There is a cooperative relationship between RNA structure and SREs in driving splicing outcome.
source: The regression model we developed clarifies that there is a cooperative relationship between RNA structure and SREs in driving splicing outcome.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Exonic non-synonymous mutations promote splicing changes primarily by altering SRE motifs.
source: Exonic non-synonymous mutations promote splicing changes primarily by altering SRE motifs, whereas exonic synonymous and intronic mutations altered RNA structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Exonic synonymous and intronic mutations altered RNA structure.
source: Exonic non-synonymous mutations promote splicing changes primarily by altering SRE motifs, whereas exonic synonymous and intronic mutations altered RNA structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: It was previously proposed that exon 10 is alternatively spliced due to a weak 5' splice site.
source: It was previously proposed that exon 10 is alternatively spliced due to a weak 5' splice site (D'Souza and Schellenberg, 2005), and indeed, we found that mutations that strengthened the splice site increase inclusion of exon 10 (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to D'Souza and Schellenberg, 2005.

claim: Mutations that strengthened the splice site increase inclusion of exon 10.
source: It was previously proposed that exon 10 is alternatively spliced due to a weak 5' splice site (D'Souza and Schellenberg, 2005), and indeed, we found that mutations that strengthened the splice site increase inclusion of exon 10 (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SRE strength alterations overall skewed more toward increased exon 10 inclusion.
source: SRE strength alterations overall skewed more toward increased exon 10 inclusion, which suggest that SREs and the RBPs that bind them buffer the effects of RNA structure to maintain the 1:1 isoform ratio.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: SREs and the RBPs that bind them buffer the effects of RNA structure to maintain the 1:1 isoform ratio.
source: SRE strength alterations overall skewed more toward increased exon 10 inclusion, which suggest that SREs and the RBPs that bind them buffer the effects of RNA structure to maintain the 1:1 isoform ratio.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that SRE changes counter structural changes.

claim: Disease variants frequently resulted in a synergistic effect on splicing outcome.
source: Although structure and SREs had opposing effects on splicing outcomes, disease variants frequently resulted in a synergistic effect on splicing outcome.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Few VUSs were predicted to completely exclude exon 10 from the mature mRNA.
source: Few VUSs were predicted to completely exclude exon 10 from the mature mRNA. Only five VUSs had PSIs less than 0.25.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of VUSs shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Only five VUSs had PSIs less than 0.25.
source: Few VUSs were predicted to completely exclude exon 10 from the mature mRNA. Only five VUSs had PSIs less than 0.25.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of VUSs shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The model accurately predicted the effect of the three VUSs with the lowest predicted PSI.
source: Our model accurately predicted the effect of the three with the lowest predicted PSI.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental validation shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Systematic computational mutagenesis revealed a hotspot for mutations around 25–30 nucleotides downstream of the exon-intron junction that were predicted to result in production of only the 3R isoform.
source: Our systematic computational mutagenesis revealed a hotspot for mutations around 25–30 nucleotides downstream of the exon-intron junction that were predicted to result in production of only the 3R isoform (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in silico mutagenesis analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The experimentally validated VUSs with PSIs less than 0.25 were in the hotspot region.
source: Indeed, the experimentally validated VUSs with PSIs less than 0.25 were in this region.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of predicted and experimental results.

claim: RBPs that recognize SRE motifs have different binding contexts.
source: In principle, our splicing model can be extended to other exon-intron junctions, although RBPs that recognize SRE motifs have different binding contexts (Dominguez et al., 2018) and the exact binding preferences of the RBPs that regulate the junction of interest are currently unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dominguez et al., 2018.

claim: The current model does not consider structural and sequence features around the 3' splice site.
source: Another limitation is that the current model does not consider structural and sequence features around the 3' splice site (in the case of MAPT exon 10, the intron 9 – exon 10 junction) that are expected to impact exon 10 splicing regulation.
evidence: The claim is an explicit statement about a limitation of the model.

claim: The model's principal utility is in predicting the direction in which the 3R to 4R isoform ratio shifted from the WT ratio.
source: Although our model provides an exact PSI prediction for each mutation, we emphasize that its principal utility is in predicting the direction in which the 3R to 4R isoform ratio shifted from the WT ratio.
evidence: The claim is an explicit statement about the utility of the model.

claim: In brain tissue from healthy individuals, exon 10 PSIs varied between individuals and between tissues within an individual.
source: In brain tissue from healthy individuals, exon 10 PSIs varied between individuals and between tissues within an individual (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by GTEx data analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Even in individuals with progressive supranuclear palsy, a tauopathy in which MAPT variants are implicated, there was variability in exon 10 PSIs in different brain tissues.
source: Even in individuals with progressive supranuclear palsy, a tauopathy in which MAPT variants are implicated, there was variability in exon 10 PSIs in different brain tissues (Majounie et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Majounie et al., 2013.

claim: It is not clear that PSI alone is predictive of severity of disease for the broad class of tauopathies.
source: Thus, although our model combines both structural and sequence features to achieve quantitative prediction accuracy of the 3R to 4R ratio for a wide range of disease mutations (synonymous, non-synonymous, intronic, and exonic), it is not clear that PSI alone is predictive of severity of disease for the broad class of tauopathies (Majounie et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the variability observed in PSI and supported by a citation.

claim: Disease severity is compounded by other factors including gene-gene interactions and environmental factors.
source: Disease severity is compounded by other factors including gene-gene interactions and environmental factors.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about disease complexity.

claim: Many neurodegenerative diseases are caused by mutations around the MAPT exon 10 – intron 10 junction.
source: Many neurodegenerative diseases are caused by mutations around the MAPT exon 10 – intron 10 junction, and there are no approved therapeutics that target this junction.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about MAPT and neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: There are no approved therapeutics that target the MAPT exon 10 – intron 10 junction.
source: Many neurodegenerative diseases are caused by mutations around the MAPT exon 10 – intron 10 junction, and there are no approved therapeutics that target this junction.
evidence: The claim is based on current knowledge about available therapeutics.

claim: It is crucial to consider the larger structural context of this region of the pre-mRNA and the interplay between structure and SREs when considering the consequences of mutations on splicing regulation and the design of potential therapeutics to alter this ratio.
source: Our work suggests that it is crucial to consider the larger structural context of this region of the pre-mRNA and the interplay between structure and SREs when considering the consequences of mutations on splicing regulation and the design of potential therapeutics to alter this ratio.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.
